A Problem of Divisibility

DivisibilityNumber TheoryAlgebra
Game: A grid of digits makes a number out of every row and every column, and the ones a chosen number divides are lit green; there is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Press a digit to raise it by one, or select it and type a digit. Change the size or the number p, and try to light all but one.

Look for the math

Write digits in a rectangle. Every row is a number, and so is every column. Pick a p with no factor in common with 10 (odd, and not a multiple of 5: 3, 7, 9, 11, 21 …). The surprise: if all of those numbers but one are divisible by p, the last one is too.

Two ways to add the same number

Weight the rows by 10n−1, 10n−2, …, 1 and add them to get C; weight the columns by 10m−1, …, 1 and add them to get D. A digit in row i and column j is multiplied by 10m+n−i−j in both sums, so C = D. The logic test confirmed this for every matrix of the three smallest shapes and for 200,000 random matrices up to 8 by 8.

Dividing out the powers of ten

Suppose every number but one is divisible by p. Then in C = D everything but one term is a multiple of p, so that term, a power of ten times the odd one out, is too. Since p and 10 are coprime, so are p and every power of 10, and the power of ten can be divided out. The test tried every matrix of the three smallest shapes and every such p up to 99, and never found exactly one number left over.

Why p must be prime to 10

Try p = 2 or p = 5. Whether a number is even depends only on its last digit, so a matrix with the first row ending in an odd digit and everything else ending in even digits leaves exactly one odd number. The claim needs p prime to 10, and the page says so.

The applet itself shows only the matrix, with clickable digits and the two sizes; the row and column integers and the number p are added here to let you test the claim, as the page asks.

Set p to 3 and try to make all rows divisible by 3 but only some columns. What does the digit sum tell you?
